value.overview: The Talamanca Hummingbird (Eugenes spectabilis) is a large hummingbird of the high mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is a striking member of the mountain-gem group and was formerly treated as the southern form of the Magnificent Hummingbird. Males show a dark head with iridescent purple and turquoise areas, while females are more subdued and mottled. The species is regularly seen in suitable cloud-forest habitats and often visits hummingbird feeders.
value.classification: The Talamanca Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the mountain-gem tribe Lampornithini. It is one of two currently recognized species in the genus Eugenes.
value.identification: This is a very large hummingbird, about 13 cm long. Adult males are mainly green, with a dark-looking head that can show a brilliant purple crown and turquoise throat in good light. Females are duller, with grayish, mottled underparts, green sides, and a conspicuous white spot behind the eye that extends into a pale eyeline. Females usually have a somewhat longer, slightly more downcurved bill. Immature birds resemble females but have buff-edged, scaly-looking plumage.
value.rangeHabitat: The Talamanca Hummingbird is restricted to highland Central America, occurring in Costa Rica and extending into western Panama near Volcán Barú. In Costa Rica, it is found in the Cordillera Central and Cordillera de Talamanca, generally from about 2,000 m to treeline, with most records above 2,500 m and occasional birds as low as roughly 1,850 m. It favors montane oak forest, mossy cloud forest, forest edges, clearings, nearby secondary growth, and highland gardens.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally a resident, non-migratory species in Costa Rica. Some individuals may make local or seasonal movements to lower elevations or between flowering areas, but there is no known regular long-distance migration.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding activity is reported mainly from November through March. The nest is a small cup made from plant fibers and other fine materials, often decorated with moss and lichens. It is typically placed on a dangling stem, such as bamboo, above the ground. Detailed information on incubation and nesting success remains limited, but young remain in the nest for at least about 25 days after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: The Talamanca Hummingbird feeds chiefly on nectar from a variety of flowering plants in montane forests and adjacent gardens. Males commonly defend productive flower patches, especially in the lower forest levels, while females often forage by trap-lining along repeated routes between flowering plants. It may also take small arthropods, although its insect-feeding behavior is less well documented than its nectar feeding.
value.behavior: Males are territorial around favored flower patches and may chase other hummingbirds during disputes. The species forages in forest understory, edges, clearings, and sometimes the canopy. It is often attracted to hummingbird feeders in Costa Rican mountain lodges and gardens. Its flight is powerful and direct, and its large size makes it distinctive among the hummingbirds of the Talamancan highlands.

conservation.populationTrend: The population size is not well known, but the overall trend is considered stable and the species remains fairly common in suitable high-elevation habitat.
